Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:1: First we must explain the essence of fear [of Heaven], and afterward the things through which a person acquires fear in his heart. This is the fear we were commanded concerning in the Torah several times (Deuteronomy 11:11) "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear the Lord your God," and likewise (ibid. 11:19) "You shall fear the Lord your God," and many like it. The reason is that once a person knows that the world has one Creator, who created all existing things and guides them as He wills, and that without His influence and vitality they would have no existence, as it is written (Nehemiah 9:6) "and You give life to them all" - and were it, God forbid, conceivable that His influence be withheld from all the worlds even for a single moment, they would all cease to be and become as though they had never existed, since they all need Him while He needs none of them - he is obligated to fear Him and accept upon himself the yoke of Torah and the yoke of the commandments, like a servant who knows he has a master and lord, [and knows] whom he serves; for if he does not know whom he serves, service will not take root in his heart, as it is written (I Chronicles 28:9) "Know the God of your father and serve Him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:2: This fear was explained by Rashbi, may he rest in peace, in the portion of Bereishit (Zohar, Bereishit 11b): "Fear is the root, for a person to fear his Master, because He is great and rules; He is the root and source of all worlds, and everything is as nothing before Him, as is said (Daniel 5:6) 'and all the inhabitants of the earth are counted as nothing'; and one should set his desire in that place which is called fear" - so far his words, as relevant to us. These words of his, small in quantity but great in quality, require lengthy explanation, and will be explained, with God's help, according to our poor understanding, following the plain sense that truly emerges from the whole of his words toward our purpose: that the essence of fear is to fear the Cause of all causes and the Reason of all reasons, who is the root and source of all the worlds - meaning that He is the One who sustains them by His life-force, blessed be He, which flows into them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:3: This is the first commandment we were commanded in the Torah: to know that there is a God, as it is said (Exodus 20:2) "I am the Lord your God." This commandment is the foundation of all foundations and the very essence of everything - to know that there is a First Existent Being who brought all existing things into being and who sustains them by His supernal influence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:4: Likewise Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, when he came to speak to Israel in Egypt to draw them toward the service of God, said (Exodus 6:7) "and I will take you to Me as a people, and I will be to you a God, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God," etc. And Rashbi, peace be upon him, wrote in the Pekudin printed in the portion of Vaera (Zohar II 25a) that this is the first commandment by which Israel were commanded to recognize the Holy One, blessed be He, in general - his words: "The very first of all commandments is to know Him, the Holy One, blessed be He, in general - to know that there is a supreme ruling power who is Master of the world and created all the worlds, heaven and earth and all their hosts; this is 'in general.'" And he explains further on that this is fear in general, but there is also a particular fear, of which it is said (Proverbs 1:7) "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge," etc., meaning the grasp of His actions and His governance through His supernal attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:5: At the giving of the Torah, Israel longed to know and see whom they served, and they said to Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, "We wish to see our King," as our Sages of blessed memory explained. The Holy One, blessed be He, granted their request and opened to them all the worlds, and they heard and saw the Voice saying "I am the Lord your God." So, too, it is explained briefly in the Tikkunim (64b): "There is no place above or below that was not spoken to, even among the angels; there is no other god in the world speaking from a throne" - this is the meaning of "I [Anokhi]," and thus Anokh"i sums to the numerical value of Kiss"e [throne], and afterward He spoke among the angels, as is said (Exodus 20:15) 'and all the people saw the voices,' about whom it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:20) 'for a bird of the heavens will carry the voice,' etc. For when the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to speak to the angels, His Name descended upon them in the form of YHVH, etc., and this is [the meaning of] 'and all the people saw the voices' - these were angels, each of which became a voice and flew through the air, and each of Israel who said 'we will do and we will hear' had it resting in his mouth, and it taught him the whole Torah; and afterward He spoke with them from heaven and earth, as is said (Deuteronomy 4:36) 'from heaven He made you hear His voice to instruct you, and on earth He showed you His great fire,' etc. Afterward He spoke with them from the four directions, and they would look toward the east and hear the voice, and toward west, north, and south they would hear the voice, to show that from every place He spoke with them, and there was no place above or below that did not speak with them, to show that His glory fills the whole earth - that He bears the upper and lower worlds, He supports above and below, the throne of glory, the angels, and the souls; He bears all, binds all, and unifies all, and there is none who supports Him" - so far, as relevant to us. And we have skipped over what was not needed for our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:6: With this we understand the verse (Deuteronomy 4:35) "You have been shown, to know that the Lord is God; there is none else besides Him" - meaning, You have been shown, for with our own eyes we saw the reality of prophecy and knew that the Lord is God, that is, the mighty God, Master and Lord of the world, and there is none else besides Him. This is what the Targum [Onkelos] renders: "for the Lord is God," for [the word] Eloha denotes the infinite Godhead, King of kings of kings. So, too, is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna, portion of Pinchas (258a): "Elohim testifies to His own divinity, for there is [a plurality called] elohim and there is the God of gods, and He is God over all and there is no god over Him" - so far his words; this is the plain sense of the verse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:7: Let us come to explain the statement in the portion of Bereishit with which we began, that the essence of fear is to fear one's Master because He is great and rules, etc. We need to know what "great" means and what "ruling" means, since these matters bear on the subject of fear.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:8: We find in our holy Torah that when it comes to ascribe fear, it ascribes fear to YHVH, as it says (Deuteronomy 11:11-12 [context]) "what does YHVH your God ask of you but to fear YHVH your God," and likewise (ibid. 11:19) "you shall fear the Lord your God and Him shall you serve," etc., and likewise (ibid. 28:58) "if you do not observe to do all the words of this Torah... to fear this glorious and awesome Name, the Lord your God." And it is known that He and His Name are one, as is known even more clearly to those who know the secret wisdom. Since this is so, whatever attribute is found suitable to be ascribed to the Lord's name, greatness and rulership, is fittingly ascribed to Him, blessed be He. And we find that YHVH is called "great," as is said (Psalms 145:3) "Great is the Lord and greatly praised, and His greatness is unsearchable." Since He is called great, it is fitting that we inquire in what respects He is called great.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:9: We find "great" in the verses used in various senses. The first is in the sense of great illumination, elevation, and spirituality, as with the two great luminaries, whose greatness was in their illumination - proof being that they are afterward called the greater light and the lesser light, denoting greatness and smallness of illumination, for the moon's light was diminished. Greatness of rank - "and the high priest [literally: the great priest] among his brothers" (Leviticus 21:10), and likewise, "the greatness of Mordechai, whom the king had made great" (Esther 10:2). Greatness of spirituality and importance - this is what David said to Saul (I Samuel 26:24) "as your soul was great [precious] this day... so let my soul be great in the eyes of the Lord"; and greatness cannot apply to the soul except in the sense of spiritual greatness and importance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:10: The second sense of "great" is in the sense of comprehension, as in (Psalms 104:25) "this sea, great [and wide]" - for if the intent were vastness of quantity, it already says "and wide of hands"; rather, it certainly means great in the sense of its depth, for there are places in the sea that have no bottom. Similarly, David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 92:6) "How great are Your works, O Lord; very deep are Your thoughts" - meaning that in the physical creation, in matters such as heaven, earth, sea, and the other great creatures, we marvel and say "how great," yet how much more exalted, in proportion, is that which cannot be grasped in its greatness and spirituality within thought, for it certainly has no measure. Hence it says "very deep are Your thoughts," and everywhere the word "very" [me'od] is used it denotes the unmeasurable, as is explained in the Zohar, portion of Vaera (27a). From the greatness of the creatures He created, we ascend by many degrees to the greatness of our Creator, the Maker of all, whose greatness our comprehension cannot reach an end or limit of.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:11: The third sense is in respect of the spreading of His power and light among created beings, as in (Numbers 14:17) "and now, let the power of the Lord be great," and likewise "with great power and a strong hand," as is explained in the portion of Shelach Lecha, and from this is derived (Exodus 14:31) "and Israel saw the great hand" - meaning the greatness of power and capability. The fourth is the greatness of kindness and mercy, as in (Numbers 14:19) "pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people according to the greatness of Your kindness," and likewise (Isaiah 54:7) "and with great mercies I will gather you." The fifth is greatness of counsel, as is said (Jeremiah 32:19) "great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:12: These five aspects contained in the word "great" are all to be ascribed to the Cause of all causes, to His exaltedness. The first, that He is great in the sense of illumination, is an illumination that has no end or limit, so that all the luminaries in the whole upper world - and how much more so what is beneath it - are all darkness compared to Him, as is explained in the Tikkunim (135b): "the supernal crown, though it is primordial light, pure light, polished light, is dark before the Cause of all causes." And it says further, "and before the Cause of all causes no light stands; all polished lights grow dark before Him" - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:13: If in the sense of the depth of comprehension: for this He, blessed be He, is called Ein Sof [Infinite], for there is no end to comprehending Him - unlike all created things, where every effect can eventually grasp its cause over the course of time; but the Cause above all, blessed be He, from the day the world was created and before, no one has ever attained the depth of comprehending Him. So too it is explained in the portion of Vayera (Zohar 103a), on the verse (Proverbs 31:23) "known in the gates is her husband": "Come and see, the Holy One, blessed be He, is exalted in His glory, for He is hidden and concealed in an exceeding loftiness beyond anything in the world; and there has not been, from the day the world was created, one who could attain His wisdom, nor could stand upon it, because He is hidden and concealed and raised up above and above, and all the upper and lower beings cannot cleave to Him until they all say 'Blessed is the glory of the Lord from His place'" - so far his words. And from the plain sense of these words there is proof for our purpose, though this statement's words are profound.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:14: Likewise, the spreading of His light among created beings - this is simply that the Cause above all shines within the ten sefirot of Atzilut, etc., as is explained in the Tikkunim (3b). And likewise the greatness of mercy - He is the source of mercy, for "in the light of the King's face is life"; and if even in the first emanated being we exclude judgment from it, how much more so in the Cause above all causes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:15: The matter of "great in counsel" may be understood from what is said in the portion of Bereishit (Zohar, Bereishit 22b) concerning "Let us make man" - his words, briefly: "What is meant by (Deuteronomy 32:39) 'See now that I, I am He'? Rather, this is the Cause of causes, the cause of all causes above, for that which is called the Cause of causes is the cause of all these causes, such that none of these causes performs any act until it takes permission from the one above it, as we established above regarding 'Let us make man' - 'let us make' was indeed said about two, meaning that this one says to the one above him, 'let us make,' and the one above him does nothing until he takes counsel from his fellow. But the one who is called the Cause of all causes, above whom there is nothing, and below whom there is none equal to Him, as it is said (Isaiah 40:25) 'To whom then will you liken Me, that I should be equal?' - He says, 'See now that I, I am He, and there is no god with Me,' who would take counsel from Him" - so far, as relevant to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:16: The reason that all these matters are ascribed to YHVH rather than to the other Names is that the Name YHVH is the source and root of all the [other] Names, as is explained in Sabba, portion of Mishpatim (Sabba, Mishpatim 96a), and further in the Tikkunim, Tikkun 57, at its end (91b-92a), this matter is explained even more clearly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:17: Further, it is explained there concerning the greatness of the Name YHVH, which we are compelled to bring over into our discussion - his words: "There is no angel in whom the Name YHVH is not found, for it is found in every place, like the soul that is found in every limb and organ; and therefore a person must proclaim the sovereignty of YHVH in every sefirah, in every throne, in every angel, and in every limb of a person, for there is no place empty of Him, neither above nor below. YHVH is not called by the unity of the four letters except through the Cause of causes who unifies them, and because He unifies the four letters within Himself, they are called YHVH in one unity - 'YHVH is one and His Name is one.' And therefore the faith of Israel is set in these four letters, and all [other divine] names are set as appellations for this Name; there is no name, up to the Infinite and to the endless, greater and more sovereign than this one, above it to the Infinite and below to the endless, and all the hosts and camps tremble and quake before it" - so far his words. Here it is explicitly stated that all the Names, even the Name Ehyeh, which belongs to Keter, are appellations of the Name YHVH, as he said, "and all [other] names are set as appellations for this Name." And he says afterward, "there is no name... greater and more sovereign than this one" - here it is explicitly stated that greatness and rulership are ascribed to YHVH more than to any other Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:18: With this the verse "Great is the Lord and greatly praised," with which we began, is explained: "Great is the Lord" - His greatness is in the respects mentioned, which stem from His kindness. "And greatly praised" - this is according to what has been explained in this discourse and will be explained further below, that through the Name YHVH all the upper and lower worlds came into existence and were created; therefore each and every one praises the Lord, blessed be He, according to its comprehension of the power of YHVH that has spread within it. The lower beings of this world praise Him according to the shortness of their comprehension, because they are in the physical realm of Asiyah, while the world of the spheres, being more refined, praises Him more; and so on from world to world, for the closer one draws to the King, the more one perceives His greatness and the might of His power. The rule is that according to the coarseness of the matter within each being, comprehension is diminished, and according to the refinement of the matter, comprehension increases; and this is "greatly praised" - for the multitude of the worlds is beyond number, and He is praised by each of them according to its comprehension. "And His greatness" - the greatness of the Name in respect of Himself, before His greatness spreads to the lower beings, is unsearchable; and when it does spread, each one praises according to its comprehension in searching out His greatness, blessed be He, insofar as it has spread within it. There is more to explain here, but we shall not lengthen further so as not to stray from the discourse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:19: Likewise we find in the Scriptures that rulership is ascribed to this Name, in the words of the Psalmist, peace be upon him (Psalms 22:29) "for the kingship is the Lord's, and He rules over the nations." Likewise in Chronicles (I Chronicles 29:11) "Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power and the glory," etc., "Yours, O Lord, is the kingdom, and You are exalted as head above all, and the riches and the honor come from before You, and You rule over all."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:20: The reason rulership is ascribed to Him after all the aforementioned attributes were mentioned is explained by Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the passage we quoted: that YHVH is the inner life-force spreading within all the worlds, like the soul that spreads through the body so that there is no place empty of it - so too YHVH is the "sap of the tree," as is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar 17a) in the discourse of Elijah. This is the matter of rulership ascribed to Him: just as the soul is what gives a person wisdom, understanding, knowledge, power, and the other attributes found in a person, which are the essence of rulership in a person, since all of them are enacted through the soul - so the Name YHVH is the ruling power to enact all actions, and everything comes from Him through the Cause of causes who unifies everything bound up in Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:21: Further, rulership is ascribed to YHVH in another respect, in the words of the Psalmist, peace be upon him, when he says (Psalms 103:20-22) "Bless the Lord, His angels, mighty in strength, who do His word," etc., "Bless the Lord, all His hosts, His ministers," etc., "Bless the Lord, all His works, in all places of His dominion." To explain the meaning of "in all places of His dominion," we must explain these three verses briefly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:22: The matter can be understood from what was explained at the beginning of the previous passage, that there is no angel in whom the Name YHVH is not found, for the Name YHVH is found in every place, and it says, "and therefore a person must proclaim the sovereignty of YHVH in every sefirah, in every throne, in every angel." We find that in the world of the Throne, YHVH is present just as in Atzilut, and likewise in the world of angels, and likewise in Asiyah, in every limb of a person. As for how YHVH may be found in every limb, it can be as is explained in the Tikkunim (139b), that every limb contains the four elements. It is further explained there (140a) that every limb contains skin, flesh, sinews, and bones, and it is explained there that upon flesh, sinews, and bones rest blessing, holiness, and unity, and these three are known to correspond to the secret of Yud-Vav, and it is further explained there that the skin is the image of man - Malchut - in which all images are seen, etc.; this corresponds to the final Heh.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:23: The matter of YHVH being found in all creatures is explained in another way in Ra'aya Meheimna, portion of "Bo el Par'oh" (42a) - his words: "All living beings that are 'holy creatures' are called by the letters of the Holy Name, as it is said (Isaiah 43:7) 'all that is called by My Name, and for My glory I have created it'; and even all creatures were created with them, and there is no creature that is not marked with this Name, so that it may be known who created it. And this is the Yud - the image of the head of all creatures; the Heh-Heh - the image of the five fingers of the right hand and the five of the left; the Vav - the image of the body; and therefore, 'to whom will you liken Me and be equal,' says the Holy One, there is no creature equal to Me, even though I created it in the likeness of My own letters, for I can erase that form and remake it as many times [as I wish]," etc. - so far, as relevant to us. Here it is explicitly stated in this passage that all His creatures are stamped with the seal of His Name, blessed be He, to show that one Creator made them, and that He rules over them to erase their form as He wills, like clay in the hand of the potter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:24: With this introduction, we shall explain the verses "Bless the Lord, His angels." In the Zohar, portion of Lech Lecha (90a), it explains that "His angels" refers to the righteous, and his words are: "Another explanation: 'Bless the Lord, His angels' - these are the righteous on earth, who are considered before the Holy One, blessed be He, like the supernal angels in the firmament, since they are 'mighty in strength,' overcoming their evil inclination like a mighty man overcoming his enemies, 'to hear the voice of His word,' for they merit every day to hear a voice from above whenever they need it" - so far, as relevant to us. Now it is known that the souls of the righteous are hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory; therefore, corresponding to the world of the Throne, whence the souls come, it says "Bless the Lord, His angels," meaning that they should draw down from Him abundance and blessing, for He is the source of blessing, as is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar 30b), that YHVH is called Baru"kh [Blessed]; "His angels" are the souls of the righteous created through YHVH, who is the seal stamped in the Throne, as it says (Isaiah 43:7) "all that is called by My Name, and for My glory I have created it."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:25: And corresponding to the third seal, stamped in the angels, it says "Bless the Lord, all His hosts, His ministers who do His will" - these are the angels who are spiritual beings above, without an evil inclination, and therefore they always do His will; and it says "bless the Lord," meaning that they should draw down abundance from YHVH, through whom they were created, as is explained in the preceding passages.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:26: "Bless YHVH, all His works" corresponds to the fourth seal, stamped in the world of the spheres, in the twelve constellations, the seven wandering stars, all the [other] stars, and all the creatures of the lower worlds - all of which are stamped with the seal of YHVH, as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna in the passage we quoted, that there is no creature that is not marked with this Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:27: And it says "in all places of His dominion," lest you say that this holds true only for the upper spiritual beings, in whom YHVH is found, but as for the lower physical beings, how could they bless YHVH? Therefore it says "in all places of His dominion," meaning that His dominion, blessed be He, is equal in all - in the lower beings as in the upper - and therefore it says, "Bless the Lord, O my soul," even though the soul is below, clothed in physicality.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:28: Further, "in all places of His dominion" - which seems superfluous, since once the whole reality of the worlds is mentioned, it is obvious that it is in all places of His dominion - rather, the intent is to include what lies between one world and another, as is explained in the Talmud (Chagigah 13a), that from the earth to the firmament is a journey of five hundred years, and likewise between one firmament and another, and in the same way between Asiyah and Yetzirah, and between Yetzirah and Beriah, etc. - all of this is "in all places of His dominion," and this is what is explained in the Tikkunim (91b), that there is no place empty of Him, neither above nor below. This is a second aspect of the dominion ascribed to YHVH: that His dominion, blessed be He, spreads through all the worlds and through all the creatures of the lower realms, all of which are stamped with His seal.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:29: This is what Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Deuteronomy 4:39) "And you shall know this day, and take it to your heart, that the Lord, He is God, in the heavens above and upon the earth beneath - there is none else." The plain meaning of "He is God" is that He is the mighty God who rules and governs over all, for every [use of] Elohim denotes strength, as in "and the mighty ones [eilei] of the land." "In the heavens above" includes the whole reality of the upper worlds up to the very highest, hence "above" - lest one say only "in the heavens" alone. "And upon the earth" - this refers to what is between heaven and earth, and what is between one earth and another, hence "and upon the earth" without qualification. "Beneath" - to include the six [lower] earths and all the creatures of the lower worlds within them. "There is none else" - for all of them came into being through the upper and lower [aspects of the Name].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:30: Now that we know this matter of dominion ascribed to YHVH, this very dominion is to be ascribed to the Cause of all causes who unifies the letters of YHVH, just as the author of the passage on fear ascribed dominion to Him, blessed be He, when he said, "fear is the root, to fear one's Master, because He is great and rules, He is the root," etc. This means that His light spreads through all the worlds, as it says in the Tikkunim (3b): "and the Cause above all shines within the ten sefirot of Atzilut, and within the ten of Beriah, and shines within the ten ranks of angels, and within the ten spheres of the firmament, and does not change in any place." We find that His illumination, blessed be He, in each and every world comes through His clothing Himself in the letters of YHVH, as was explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:31: And when it says "and does not change in any place," lest one say "and does not change" alone - for "in any place" would seemingly refer to the places already mentioned, which were said to be the ten of Atzilut, etc. Rather, it appears to be along the lines of "in all places of His dominion" in the second explanation. We thus learn that even in the air of the world, the Cause of all causes is found, clothed in the letters of YHVH, who is one with His Name; and this is the essence of the fear of which Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, spoke (Deuteronomy 28:58): "to fear this glorious and awesome Name, YHVH your God" - and he says "this" only as one who points with a finger, indicating that He is present before us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:32: Now, by this we understand the secret of "the whole earth is full of His glory," as explained in Ra'aya Meheimna, portion "Bo el Par'oh" (42b), that this refers to the spreading of the supernal Godhead - his words: "For if His light did not spread over all creatures, how would they come to know Him, and how would 'the whole earth is full of His glory' be fulfilled?" - so far his words. And for this reason David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 16:8) "I have set the Lord before me always," for by thinking that YHVH is before him - there, in that place, is the Cause of all causes who unifies everything - from this comes to a person awe, shame, and modesty, that he should not sin before the supreme King, glorious and awesome, who is before him, as these words will be further explained, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:33: Now that we have explained the meaning of "great" and "ruling," we must explain what fear results for a person from this. The matter is: from His being great, in the manner we explained, fear results - a person should feel shame on account of His greatness, which has no end, whether in the aspect of great illumination, as will be explained in the next chapter, or in the aspect of His being great in counsel and mighty in deed, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:34: And from His being a ruler, this indicates providence, as I have explained, and further, that He rules over the two hundred and forty-eight limbs [of a person], which are stamped with His Name; and if one sins with them, he is found to be blemishing YHVH, "the root and source of all worlds" (Zohar I 11b) - meaning that His essence and His flow sustain them, as is said (Nehemiah 9:6) "and You give life to them all," and as was explained in the passage we recently quoted, "and the Cause above all shines," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:35: This is the essence of faith: to know that if, God forbid, it were conceivable that there were no God in the world, there would be no existence of a world at all, and it would not have been created; and since there is a world with created beings within it, they must have one Creator who created them and guides them as He wills. All created beings are like the image of a tree that lives only from its roots - so, too, all created beings live only through the Cause of all causes, who is the root sustaining everything. There is more to say on this, but there is no room here to elaborate.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:36: This aspect, too, was revealed through the Name YHVH, for this Name is the inner life-force spreading through all the worlds, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the passage from the Tikkunim we quoted above, saying "there is no angel in whom the Name YHVH is not found," etc.; and even in the sun the Name YHVH is clothed, as is explained in the Tikkunim (145a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:37: "And everything is as nothing before Him" (ibid., continuing, Zohar I 11b) - this bears on the essence of faith: that if the non-existence of all created beings were conceivable, no deficiency would thereby befall His greatness, blessed be He, for He was called King even before the world was created, as it is said (Proverbs 8:26) "while He had not yet made earth or open places, the Lord was King"; and everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory, so that His greatness would be recognized, as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna. And even at the end of all things (Isaiah 34:4) "and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll, and all their host shall wither... and YHVH alone shall be exalted on that day."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:38: At the time of man's creation, our Sages of blessed memory said that the angels who protested against the creation of man - He put forth His finger among them and burned them, showing, by way of illustration, that they are all of no account before Him, blessed be He, to annul them as though they had never been.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:39: From this follow two additional aspects of fear, beyond those already stated regarding "great" and "ruling." The first: since a person's life comes from Him, blessed be He, as we explained, he must feel shame before Him not to sin with the life He infuses within him, and he should fear, for "His spirit and soul He will gather to Himself; all flesh will perish together" (Job 34:14-15). And so said Daniel (5:23), "and to the God in whose hand is your breath, and all your ways, you have not glorified Him." By reflecting on this matter, a person greatly purifies his thoughts.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 1:40: The second: although He has no need of created beings, nevertheless His providence watches over them to do them good, as is said (Psalms 145:9) "and His mercies are upon all His works." Let a person say in his heart: "What recompense shall I pay my Creator, blessed be He, for all His goodness that overflows to me every day, if I transgress His will?" Rather, it is fitting that I perform His commandments to bring Him satisfaction. This matter was explained by my teacher, peace be upon him, in his explanation of the passage regarding "and everything is as nothing before Him."
